source: The season for the Line at length drew near; and every day when Ahab, coming from his cabin, cast his eyes aloft, the vigilant helmsman would ostentatiously handle his spokes, and the eager mariners quickly run to the braces, and would stand there with all their eyes centrally fixed on the nailed doubloon; impatient for the order to point the ship’s prow for the equator. In good time the order came. It was hard upon high noon; and Ahab, seated in the bows of his high-hoisted boat, was about taking his wonted daily observation of the sun to determine his latitude.

Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are as freshets of effulgences. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean’s immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; clouds there are none; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is as the insufferable splendors of God’s throne. Well that Ahab’s quadrant was furnished with coloured glasses, through which to take sight of that solar fire. So, swinging his seated form to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument placed to his eye, he remained in that posture for some moments to catch the precise instant when the sun should gain its precise meridian. Meantime while his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship’s deck, and with face thrown up like Ahab’s, was eyeing the same sun with him; only the lids of his eyes half hooded their orbs, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil upon his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then falling into a moment’s revery, he again looked up towards the sun and murmured to himself: “Thou sea-mark! thou high and mighty Pilot! thou tellest me truly where I am—but canst thou cast the least hint where I shall be? Or canst thou tell where some other thing besides me is this moment living? Where is Moby Dick? This instant thou must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, thither side of thee, thou sun!”

Then gazing at his quadrant, and handling, one after the other, its numerous cabalistical contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: “Foolish toy! babies’ plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of thee, of thy cunning and might; but what after all canst thou do, but tell the poor, pitiful point, where thou thyself happenest to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds thee: no! not one jot more! Thou canst not tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be to-morrow noon; and yet with thy impotence thou insultest the sun! Science! Curse thee, thou vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man’s eyes aloft to that heaven, whose live vividness but scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with thy light, O sun! Level by nature to this earth’s horizon are the glances of man’s eyes; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse thee, thou quadrant!” dashing it to the deck, “no longer will I guide my earthly way by thee; the level ship’s compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line; these shall conduct me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye,” lighting from the boat to the deck, “thus I trample on thee, thou paltry thing that feebly pointest on high; thus I split and destroy thee!”

As the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live and dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself—these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee’s face. Unobserved he rose and glided away; while, awestruck by the aspect of their commander, the seamen clustered together on the forecastle, till Ahab, troubledly pacing the deck, shouted out—“To the braces! Up helm!—square in!”

In an instant the yards swung round; and as the ship half-wheeled upon her heel, her three firm-seated graceful masts erectly poised upon her long, ribbed hull, seemed as the three Horatii pirouetting on one sufficient steed.
Standing between the knight-heads, Starbuck watched the Pequod’s tumultuous way, and Ahab’s also, as he went lurching along the deck.

“I have sat before the dense coal fire and watched it all aglow, full of its tormented flaming life; and I have seen it wane at last, down, down, to dumbest dust. Old man of oceans! of all this fiery life of thine, what will at length remain but one little heap of ashes!”

“Aye,” cried Stubb, “but sea-coal ashes—mind ye that, Mr. Starbuck—sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab mutter, ‘Here some one thrusts these cards into these old hands of mine; swears that I must play them, and no others.’ And damn me, Ahab, but thou actest right; live in the game, and die in it!”

modern_en.title: Chapter 118 — The Quadrant
paragraphs: The season for the Line, the equator, finally came close. Every day, whenever Ahab came up from his cabin and looked aloft, the watchful helmsman would make a show of handling his spokes, and the eager sailors would hurry to the braces and stand there with all their eyes converging on the nailed doubloon, impatient for the order to point the ship's prow toward the equator. In due time the order came. It was nearly high noon, and Ahab, seated in the bow of his boat, which was hoisted high, was about to take his usual daily sighting of the sun to find his latitude.

Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; there are no clouds; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is like the unbearable splendors of God's throne. It was well that Ahab's quadrant, the instrument for measuring the sun's height, was fitted with colored glasses through which to sight that solar fire. So, swinging his seated body to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument to his eye, he held that posture for some moments to catch the exact instant when the sun should reach its precise meridian. Meanwhile, as his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship's deck, and with his face thrown up like Ahab's, was eyeing the same sun with him; only his eyelids half hooded his eyes, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil on his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then, falling into a moment's reverie, he looked up again toward the sun and murmured to himself: "You sea-mark! You high and mighty Pilot! You tell me truly where I am now — but can you cast the least hint of where I shall be? Or can you tell where some other thing besides me is living this moment? Where is Moby Dick? This instant you must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, far side of you, you sun!"

Then, gazing at his quadrant and handling one after another its many cabalistic contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Babies' plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what, after all, can you do, except tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds you — no! not one jot more! You cannot tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be tomorrow noon; and yet with your impotence you insult the sun! Science! Curse you, you vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose live vividness only scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with your light, O sun! By nature, the glances of man's eyes are level with this earth's horizon; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck. "No longer will I guide my earthly way by you; the level ship's compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line — it is these that shall guide me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye," stepping down from the boat to the deck, "thus I trample on you, you paltry thing that feebly points on high; thus I split and destroy you!"

As the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live and dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself — these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee's face. Unobserved he rose and glided away; while, awestruck by the aspect of their commander, the sailors clustered together on the forecastle, until Ahab, pacing the deck in agitation, shouted out: "To the braces! Up helm! — square in!"

In an instant the yards swung around, and as the ship half-spun on her heel, her three graceful masts, firmly seated and standing upright on her long ribbed hull, looked like the three Horatii pirouetting on a single horse strong enough to carry them all.
Standing between the knightheads (the timbers on either side of the bowsprit), Starbuck watched the Pequod's tumultuous way, and Ahab's also, as he went lurching along the deck.

"I have sat by a thick coal fire and watched it glowing, full of its tormented, flaming life, and I have seen it fade at last, down, down, to the dumbest dust. Old man of the oceans! Of all this fiery life of yours, what will finally be left but one little heap of ashes!"

"Aye," cried Stubb, "but sea-coal ashes — mind you that, Mr. Starbuck — sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab mutter, 'Here someone thrusts these cards into these old hands of mine; swears that I must play them, and no others.' And damn me, Ahab, but you act right; live in the game, and die in it!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 118 — Kvadranten
paragraphs: Årstiden for Linjen, ækvator, nærmede sig endelig. Hver dag, når Ahab kom op fra sin kahyt og så op mod mastetoppene, gjorde den årvågne rorsmand stort væsen af at tage fat på rattets håndtag, og de ivrige sømænd skyndte sig hen til brasserne og stod der med alle deres øjne rettet mod den fastnaglede doblon, utålmodige efter ordren om at sætte skibets stævn mod ækvator. Til sin tid kom ordren. Det var nær ved højt middag, og Ahab, der sad i stavnen på sin båd, som var hejst højt op, var ved at tage sin sædvanlige daglige solhøjde for at finde sin bredde.

Nu er sommerens dage i det japanske hav en flod af glans. Den ublinkende, levende japanske sol ser ud som brændpunktet i det glasklare havs umådelige brændglas. Himlen ser ud, som om den var lakeret; der er ingen skyer; horisonten svæver; og denne nøgenhed af ubrudt stråleglans ligner Guds trones uudholdelige pragt. Det var godt, at Ahabs kvadrant, det instrument, der måler solens højde, var forsynet med farvede glas, så man kunne sigte mod solens ild. Så han svingede sin siddende krop med skibets rulning og holdt sit astrologiagtige instrument op til øjet, og i den stilling blev han nogle øjeblikke for at fange det nøjagtige øjeblik, hvor solen nåede sin præcise middagshøjde. Imens, da hele hans opmærksomhed var opslugt, knælede parsien under ham på skibets dæk, og med ansigtet kastet bagover som Ahabs betragtede han den samme sol sammen med ham; kun halvt dækkede øjenlågene hans øjne, og hans vilde ansigt var dæmpet til en jordisk lidenskabsløshed. Til sidst var den ønskede observation foretaget, og med sin blyant på elfenbensbenet beregnede Ahab snart, hvilken bredde han måtte befinde sig på i netop det øjeblik. Så faldt han i et kort drømmeri, så op mod solen igen og mumlede for sig selv: »Du sømærke! Du høje og mægtige lods! Du fortæller mig sandt, hvor jeg er nu — men kan du give det mindste fingerpeg om, hvor jeg skal være? Eller kan du sige, hvor noget andet end jeg lever i dette øjeblik? Hvor er Moby Dick? I dette øjeblik må du se på ham. Disse mine øjne ser ind i det øje, som selv nu ser på ham; ja, og ind i det øje, som selv nu lige så vel ser på tingene på den ukendte, fjerne side af dig, du sol!«

Så så han på sin kvadrant og rørte ved den ene efter den anden af dens mange kabbalistiske indretninger, grundede igen og mumlede: »Tåbeligt legetøj! Småbørns legetøj for stolte admiraler og kommandører og kaptajner. Verden praler af dig, af din snilde og din magt. Men hvad kan du i grunden andet end fortælle det stakkels, ynkelige punkt, hvor du selv tilfældigvis er på denne vide klode, og den hånd, der holder dig — nej! ikke en tøddel mere! Du kan ikke sige, hvor en eneste dråbe vand eller et eneste sandkorn vil være i morgen ved middagstid; og alligevel fornærmer du med din afmagt solen! Videnskab! Forbandet være du, dit forfængelige legetøj; og forbandet være alle de ting, der drager menneskets øjne op mod den himmel, hvis levende glans kun svier ham, som disse gamle øjne selv nu svies af dit lys, o sol! Af naturen er menneskets blik i højde med jordens horisont; det er ikke skudt ud fra issen af hans hoved, som om Gud havde ment, at han skulle stirre på sit himmelhvælv. Forbandet være du, kvadrant!« og han smed den ned på dækket. »Aldrig mere vil jeg styre min jordiske vej efter dig; skibets vandrette kompas og den vandrette gisning ved log og line — det er dem, der skal styre mig og vise mig, hvor jeg er på havet. Ja,« sagde han, mens han steg ned fra båden til dækket, »således træder jeg på dig, din usle lille ting, der svagt peger mod det høje; således splitter og ødelægger jeg dig!«

Mens den rasende gamle mand talte således og trampede med sit levende og sit døde ben, gled der over den tavse, ubevægelige parsis ansigt en hånlig sejrsglæde, der syntes ment for Ahab, og en skæbnetro fortvivlelse, der syntes ment for ham selv. Uset rejste han sig og gled væk. Imens samlede sømændene sig, slået af ærefrygt over deres befalingsmands udseende, i en klump på back, indtil Ahab, der gik urolig frem og tilbage på dækket, råbte: »Til brasserne! Ror op! — Brass tværs!«

I et nu svingede rærne rundt, og mens skibet næsten drejede om på hælen, så dets tre yndefulde master, der stod fast og rank på dets lange, ribbede skrog, ud som de tre Horatier, der piruetterede på en eneste hest, stærk nok til at bære dem alle.
Starbuck stod mellem knighthovederne (tømmerstykkerne på hver side af bovspryden) og så Pequods uro på sin vej, og Ahabs også, mens han slingrede hen over dækket.

»Jeg har siddet ved et tykt kulbål og set det gløde, fuldt af sit pinte, flammende liv, og jeg har set det til sidst dø ud, ned, ned til det stummeste støv. Havenes gamle mand! Hvad skal der til sidst blive tilbage af hele dit ildfulde liv andet end en lille bunke aske!«

»Ja,« råbte Stubb, »men søkulaske — husk det, Mr. Starbuck — søkul, ikke almindeligt trækul. Nå, nå; jeg hørte Ahab mumle: ›Her stikker nogen disse kort i disse mine gamle hænder; sværger på, at jeg skal spille dem og ingen andre.‹ Og for pokker, Ahab, men du gør ret; lev i spillet og dø i det!«
